title: Check if a string is a palindrome (same forwards and backwards, e.g., "madam") — compare first and last characters moving inward.
shortTitle: Check if a string is a palindrome

s1_definition.profdef: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. The efficient check uses two pointers, one at each end, comparing the characters they point at and moving inward; if any pair differs it is not a palindrome. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, which beats the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India lets Rajesh choose a short memorable code, and the UI flags codes that read the same both ways as "symmetric" for fun. A clerk checks a code by comparing the first and last letters, then the second and second-last, moving toward the middle. If every pair matches, it is a palindrome.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare the outermost characters and move inward; if every mirrored pair matches it is a palindrome.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. The efficient check uses two pointers, one at each end, comparing the characters they point at and moving inward; if any pair differs it is not a palindrome. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, which beats the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India lets Rajesh choose a short memorable code, and the UI flags codes that read the same both ways as "symmetric" for fun. A clerk checks a code by comparing the first and last letters, then the second and second-last, moving toward the middle. If every pair matches, it is a palindrome.

**One line to remember:** Compare the outermost characters and move inward; if every mirrored pair matches it is a palindrome.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer method puts `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. You compare `chars at left` with `chars at right`. If they differ, you return false immediately, because a single mismatch rules out a palindrome. If they match, you move `left` forward and `right` backward and repeat while `left < right`. If the loop completes without a mismatch, the string is a palindrome.

This is better than the naive method of reversing the string and calling equals, because the two-pointer approach exits early on the first mismatch and uses only constant extra space, whereas reversing allocates a whole new string. The early exit matters for long inputs that fail near the start.

A practical nuance is normalisation. Real palindrome checks often ignore case and non-letter characters, so "Madam" or "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" count as palindromes. You handle this by lowercasing and stripping non-alphanumeric characters before the two-pointer scan. Time stays O(n) and space is O(1) for the scan itself, though normalisation into a cleaned string costs O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's app lets Rajesh pick a short reference code and shows a playful "symmetric code" badge when the code reads the same both ways. The system must check whether a code is a palindrome. This is exactly how the palindrome check works — compare mirrored characters moving inward.

Problem 2 — Customers type codes with mixed case and spaces, but "Madam" and "madam" should both count. This is exactly why we normalise to lowercase and strip non-letter characters before comparing.

The code has a `PalindromeChecker` class with an `isPalindrome` method that normalises then does the two-pointer scan. The demo checks several codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: code `"Madam"`.

Step 1 — Normalise: lowercase to `"madam"`, strip non-letters (none here). Cleaned is `"madam"`, with `left=0`, `right=4`.

Step 2 — Compare index 0 `'m'` and index 4 `'m'`: equal. Move to `left=1`, `right=3`.

Step 3 — Compare index 1 `'a'` and index 3 `'a'`: equal. Move to `left=2`, `right=2`.

Step 4 — Now `left` is not less than `right`, loop stops. Return true.

Step 5 — For `"RAJESH"`, normalised to `"rajesh"`, the first comparison `'r'` versus `'h'` differs, so it returns false immediately. `"level"` returns true, and `"A1b2"` normalises to `"a1b2"` and returns false.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'Madam' palindrome? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'RAJESH' palindrome? false
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'level' palindrome? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'A1b2' palindrome? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: "Madam"
    │
    ▼
  PalindromeChecker.isPalindrome()
    │ normalise → "madam"   left=0 right=4
    │ m==m  left=1 right=3
    │ a==a  left=2 right=2  → stop
    ▼
  return true

  "RAJESH" → "rajesh": r==h → return false (early exit)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A palindrome is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards, and the efficient way to check one is the two-pointer technique. I place one pointer at the start and one at the end, compare the two characters, and if they differ I return false immediately. If they match, I move both pointers inward and repeat until they meet in the middle. If I never find a mismatch, the string is a palindrome. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in a small user-facing feature where the app shows a playful symmetric-code badge when a customer picks a reference code that reads the same both ways. Before I run the two-pointer scan I normalise the input by lowercasing it and stripping out anything that is not a letter or digit, so that a code typed as Madam with a capital M, or one with spaces, is still recognised correctly.

I specifically prefer the two-pointer method over the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing it with the original. The two-pointer method exits on the very first mismatched pair, which is much faster when the string fails the test early, and it uses only constant extra space, whereas reversing allocates an entire new string. That early-exit plus constant-space combination is the reason interviewers like to see the two-pointer solution rather than the reverse-and-compare shortcut.
